entries.name: Population Based Training
entries.definition: A population-based neural-network training procedure that interleaves parameter updates with performance-guided copying of partially trained models and exploration of hyperparameters, producing training trajectories with changing hyperparameter settings.
entries.identity_notes: PBT jointly trains model weights and searches hyperparameter schedules. It differs from independent random-search runs, a prediction ensemble and Population Based Augmentation’s specialized augmentation-schedule transfer. Its population updates do not require genetic crossover. General PBT can return the trained model; PBA separately discards its child weights when transferring a schedule. Reinforcement learning is one application, not the definition of PBT. limitations: The original algorithm specifies application-dependent readiness, exploitation and exploration. PBA’s quartile selection, three-epoch interval, operation probabilities and schedule-only transfer are not general PBT requirements.

claims.statement: Maintain population members with model parameters, hyperparameters, an evaluation score and training progress. Each worker trains its parameters with its current hyperparameters and evaluates a chosen performance metric, which need not be differentiable or identical to the local training objective. When a readiness condition holds, an exploitation rule can replace that worker’s parameters and hyperparameters with those of another promising member. An exploration rule then perturbs or resamples the copied hyperparameters, and training continues from the inherited weights. Algorithm 1 calls exploration and re-evaluation only when exploitation changes the weights; its final output is the population member’s parameters with the highest recorded score. Readiness, selection and mutation rules depend on the application. The original procedure is asynchronous: members need access to population scores, parameters and hyperparameters, but no population-wide synchronization barrier is required. Alternating local parameter learning with slower model selection and hyperparameter changes yields schedules along training lineages, rather than restricting each run to one fixed hyperparameter configuration.

entries.name: Tree-structured Parzen Estimator
entries.definition: A sequential hyperparameter optimization method that separates observations by a loss quantile, fits tree-structured densities for the better and remaining configurations, and proposes evaluations using their density ratio as an expected-improvement ranking.
entries.identity_notes: TPE is the particular two-density sequential optimizer introduced by Bergstra et al., not every Parzen density estimator, every expected-improvement method, Gaussian-process regression or the downstream Fast AutoAugment policy search that uses it. The quantile threshold groups observations for density fitting; it need not equal the best observed loss. Names and author order follow the inspected proceedings PDF. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 9 lines in each checkout. Fourteen exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and six neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The ratio ranking assumes the paper’s two-region conditional model and a finite, positive improvement constant. It is not the numerical value of expected improvement without that constant, nor an optimality or calibration guarantee.

The derivation after Equation (3) prints an integral without the factor y in an expanded numerator. The unexpanded integral of (y*−y)*p(y) gives the density-ratio ranking recorded here. This is an explicit source qualification, not an author-issued erratum or a claim to reproduce a software implementation.

The original tree-structured factorization encodes conditional activation and the specified density families. It does not establish arbitrary dependency modeling or identity with later multivariate TPE variants.

Prior choices, density bandwidths, quantile selection, observations and finite candidate sampling affect search. No universal efficiency, final objective improvement or benchmark advantage is asserted.

claims.statement: Represent valid configurations with a conditional generative tree so that some variables are active only for particular parent choices. Given observed configurations and losses to minimize, choose a loss threshold at a quantile gamma and fit l(x) from observations below that threshold and g(x) from the remainder. The model uses p(x|y)=l(x) below the threshold and g(x) otherwise, with p(x)=gamma*l(x)+(1−gamma)*g(x). Under this construction, expected nonnegative improvement E[max(y*−y,0)] is proportional, across configurations, to [gamma+(1−gamma)*g(x)/l(x)]^−1 wherever the relevant densities and expectation are defined. Draw candidate configurations from l, rank them by this expression, evaluate the selected candidate’s actual loss, and incorporate the observation into subsequent density estimates. The original estimator replaces continuous priors with adaptive Parzen mixtures around observed values and retains a prior component; bounded uniform variables use truncated Gaussian mixtures, log-uniform variables are modeled in log space, and categorical probabilities are reweighted by observed counts. The tree specifies conditional variable activation, not a decision tree that predicts loss. This is distinct from the separate Gaussian-process surrogate described in Section 3 of the same paper.

entries.name: Bayesian Data Augmentation for Deep Models
entries.definition: Tran et al.’s supervised deep-learning procedure that treats synthetic labeled examples as latent data, repeatedly samples them from an evolving learned model and updates model parameters through a generalized Monte Carlo expectation-maximization formulation.
entries.identity_notes: This record is scoped to the 2017 Tran et al. formulation for generating labeled deep-learning training examples. It is not all statistical Bayesian data augmentation, generic EM, Bayesian-network graphical modeling or posterior sampling of neural-network weights. Its class-conditioned generative model differs from AdaMixUp’s interpolation and cooperative intrusion discriminator. Generalized Monte Carlo EM is the formulation used here, not an alias identifying every GMCEM application with this record. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 9 lines in each checkout. limitations: The generalized M-step requires improvement of its objective. Differentiability alone does not guarantee that an arbitrary finite gradient step or a noisy minibatch epoch increases that objective.

The source’s Lemma 1 moves from a sampled-objective inequality to an expectation inequality. Improvement observed for one finite sample does not by itself guarantee improvement of the exact expected objective or the observed-data posterior, especially when the update is selected using that sample. No unconditional monotonicity or convergence guarantee for practical GAN training is asserted.

Equations (18)–(19) link authenticator losses to data log-likelihood terms. A real/fake discriminator probability is not itself a normalized data density; this record describes the published adversarial surrogate without asserting an exact normalized-likelihood or exact-EM implementation.

Separate real and synthetic means assign each group its own normalization. Increasing the number of generated samples does not automatically multiply the synthetic group’s total coefficient in the printed objective.
Generated labels and images depend on the fitted model and optimization. No label-correctness guarantee, universal sample quality, benchmark advantage or reproduction of author software is asserted.

claims.statement: Treat each additional labeled example z=(t_a,x_a) as a latent variable and seek a maximum-a-posteriori parameter estimate, rather than sampling a posterior over all network weights. At an iteration, sample synthetic labeled data using the current model and approximate the expected augmented log posterior with a Monte Carlo average. The generalized M-step seeks parameters that increase this sampled objective rather than solving a global maximization exactly. The published objective includes a parameter prior, an average of real-data label/data log terms and a separate average of synthetic-data label/data log terms. In the paper’s concrete GAN realization, a class-conditioned generator produces labeled images, a classifier learns dataset labels on real and generated examples, and a separate authenticator distinguishes real from generated images. The published discriminative step minimizes J_C+J_AG, while the generative step minimizes J_C−J_AG, combining class consistency with adversarial realism. J_C separately averages the real and synthetic classification losses, rather than averaging one pooled batch with weights determined solely by its real-to-synthetic count ratio. The practical training procedure uses minibatches and one epoch of stochastic updates per parameter-update iteration. The GAN architecture is one realization of the augmentation framework, not a requirement for every possible realization.

native_neighbors.name: Population Based Augmentation
native_neighbors.definition: An augmentation-schedule learning procedure that jointly trains a population of child classifiers and evolves their augmentation hyperparameters by copying successful members and perturbing their policies over training time.

claims.statement: Train a population of randomly initialized child classifiers and periodically compare their validation performance. In the published truncation-selection configuration, a bottom-quartile member copies the weights and augmentation hyperparameters of a top-quartile member, then perturbs those hyperparameters and continues training without reinitializing the copied weights. Each policy has two entries for each of 15 operation types, excluding SamplePairing, with one magnitude and one application probability per entry: 60 scalar hyperparameters. The probability grid is 0 to 1 in tenths and magnitude indices are 0 through 9. To augment an image, shuffle the 30 entries, draw an operation-count cap of 0,1 or 2 with probabilities 0.2,0.3 or 0.5, then scan entries and probabilistically apply each until that many operations have actually been applied or the list is exhausted. Each hyperparameter is reset uniformly with probability 0.2; otherwise its integer grid index is shifted up or down by a uniformly sampled amount in {0,1,2,3} and clipped to its domain. The source uses an epoch per step, an exploit/explore interval of three epochs and initially zero probabilities/magnitudes. Retain the selected schedule along the winning training lineage and discard the child weights when training the final model; schedules can be stretched to a different training duration. These numerical settings are the published configuration, not universal PBT requirements.

evidence.locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, Algorithms 1–2, PDF pp. 3–5; schedule initialization and transfer in Section 4.1, PDF pp. 5–6

claims.statement: The pinned exploration code stores probability indices as integers0..10 and magnitude indices as integers0..9, applies reset or signed local perturbations and clips to the matching bounds. The augmentation function decrements its sampled cap only after an operation passes its probability test, stopping at zero or the end of the shuffled list. Repeated operation types are possible because the policy contains two entries per type; applying the same type twice does not require sampling with replacement from a one-entry-per-type list.

native_neighbors.name: Fast AutoAugment
native_neighbors.definition: An augmentation-policy search procedure that evaluates candidate transformations on held-out training examples using a fixed classifier trained on another split, combines high-scoring policies across splits and uses them for final classifier training.

claims.statement: Form repeated stratified train/exploration splits. Train a classifier on each model-training split, then hold its weights fixed while exploring augmentation policies on that split’s held-out labeled examples. A subpolicy composes image operations with individual application probabilities and magnitudes; the published search uses continuous probability and normalized magnitude values in [0,1]. Use Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, implemented with a tree-structured Parzen estimator, to propose policies according to their predictive scores. The paper frames the goal as maximizing augmented-split accuracy and states that its practical objective minimizes categorical cross-entropy. Select top policies from each search stage and split, merge their subpolicies, and train the final classifier on the full training data with the selected augmentation. The published configuration uses two operations per subpolicy and five subpolicies per candidate policy, but these are protocol choices. The method uses classifier predictions as a proxy for matching distributions; it does not directly compute a distributional divergence. Its essential efficiency distinction is reuse of fixed model weights during candidate scoring, while initial and final classifier training are still required.

evidence.locator: Section 3, Equations (1)–(4), Figure 2 and Algorithm 1, PDF pp. 3–6; Section 4 setup on p. 6

claims.statement: The pinned search.py evaluates a saved model in evaluation mode on multiple stochastic augmented views of held-out examples. The active augment_list(False) contains 15 operations, with SamplePairing commented out, while the paper lists 16. The inspected search loop performs one repetition per split rather than the paper’s reported two. These are version-specific conventions, not silently combined definitions.

native_neighbors.name: AdaMixUp
native_neighbors.definition: An adaptive interpolation-training procedure that learns example-dependent mixing-coefficient regions with a policy network and trains a classifier together with an intrusion discriminator intended to separate mixed examples from original data.

claims.statement: For a pair of examples, a policy-region network outputs a three-component softmax (alpha,delta,remainder). Interpret the first two components as the interval(alpha,alpha+delta) for the mixing coefficient. Sample epsilon uniformly on(0,1) and set gamma=alpha+delta*epsilon so gradients can pass through the interval parameters. Form gamma*x1+(1−gamma)*x2 and the correspondingly mixed class targets. Train the classifier with observed and mixed targets, and train the policy generator together with an intrusion discriminator to distinguish generated mixtures from original examples. The discriminator shares the classifier’s feature network while using its own final classification layers. For higher-fold mixing, reuse the same pairwise generator recursively by mixing an original example with an original or previously mixed example; composing a previous coefficient vector lambda with coefficient gamma gives (gamma*lambda,1−gamma). The paper describes alternating minibatch optimization of classification/mixup loss and intrusion loss. Its intended intrusion supervision treats mixed examples as outside and observed examples as inside the data manifold; this is a learned surrogate, not direct access to the true manifold.

evidence.locator: Adaptive MixUp and Implementation of AdaMixUp, Equations (5)–(7), Figure 3 and Training, PDF pp. 4–6 / printed pp. 3717–3719; assumptions and intrusion boundaries on pp. 2–4

claims.statement: The pinned Fold-2 reimplementation generates interval parameters with softmax, samples gamma by reparameterization and uses the same coefficient to mix inputs and labels. Its classifier uses softmax cross-entropy over an equal-sized mixture of generated examples and one source group. Its binary intrusion head uses softmax cross-entropy, labels originals1 and mixtures0, and averages over two original groups and one mixed group. The returned cost sums the classification and intrusion means and a weight-decay term. This realizes the separation intention using negative log-probabilities, with source-specific label encoding and weighting rather than literal positive-log minimization or a demonstrated reproduction of the paper’s alternating update schedule.
